D01.why: the prose rule extended to the dimensions: 'every contributor holds the same tiny resource' is contradicted by the 236 rooms with scripts and spare accounts; 'the room reads it off the canvas and the thread' is contradicted for the thread by F-015; 'newcomers must first learn what the event is before they can count' was a causal claim that no count supports; 'the question here is not whether people free-ride, but' was a negative parallel

now.changed: Marwell and Oliver (1993, recalled) describe a critical mass of a few contributors with many resources, whose early contributions make a public good viable for the rest. Here each account could place one pixel per interval, and members multiplied their accounts with scripts and spare accounts in 236 rooms. Members judged the room's numbers by the size of its readership or by the canvas, not by who answered a call (F-015, weak). No threshold of hands has been tested.
now.mistaken_for: Olson's free-rider problem, or a tipping point (Granovetter 1978, recalled). The themes here hold calls, explanations of the canvas and judgments of the room's numbers. A read prompted by threshold models found no judgment of numbers that rested on who answered (F-015, weak).

D02.why: the prose rule extended to the dimensions: 'what joins them is the absence of command, not informality' was a negative parallel; the source is marked recalled; the rest stands on the setting (no one could order another to place) and F-006 (decided order rare)

now.mistaken_for: Mintzberg's mutual adjustment (recalled), or self-organization in general. Mutual adjustment is one of its routes, the trace on the canvas. The dimension also holds templates, scripts, chats and the rare decided order (46 of 705 rooms, F-006). What joins them is that no member could order another to place.

D03.why: the prose rule extended to the dimensions: 'it decides between quiet repair, forgiveness and retaliation' was a causal claim that the run's test contradicts (attribution then restraint at chance, attribution then attack reversed); 'no one is charged' was universal against the 24 rooms where members covered a night shift; the source is marked recalled
rests_on: model-C4.md: looked for and not found (attribution as the hinge)

now.changed: Graham and Thrift (2007, recalled) describe the routine care of infrastructures by those charged with it. Here no authority charged anyone with the care, though members in 24 rooms covered a night shift. Members report attacks, and they report changes they later find were a friend's work or their own mistake (46 rooms). Attribution was tested as the step that decides between restraint and attack, and it was not found.

D04.why: the prose rule extended to the dimensions: 'no law over the canvas at all' was universal and is restated as the setting fact; 'the shared future lasts 72 hours' is corrected to the 73 hours of placement; 'some neighbours fight for sport' is given its count; 'order is made pair by pair, not by a rule-setting body' was universal and a negative parallel, against the 146 rooms that form bodies of rooms
rests_on: structure-C4.md: rooms carrying Negotiated order (467) and Meta-organization (146); T3-192 (13 rooms)

now.changed: Ellickson (1991, recalled) describes neighbours who settle disputes by informal norms, with the law in the background and a long shared future. Here no rule of the canvas settled disputes between rooms, placement lasted 73 hours, and no room could order its placers to keep a deal. Members in 13 rooms griefed other rooms' work for fun.
now.mistaken_for: Anarchy in the international-relations sense, or the governance of a commons (Ostrom, recalled). There is no common pool to manage here, only adjacent works. Rooms carrying talk of borders, truces and deals with one other room (467) outnumber rooms carrying bodies of rooms (146).

D05.why: the prose rule extended to the dimensions: 'mostly carried in from outside' was an uncounted comparison and now carries the rooms of each theme; F-011 is written in, since membership carried in does not come before the attack more often than chance; the sources are marked recalled
rests_on: structure-C4.md: rooms carrying Frame bridging (242), Flagging the nation (62), Neo-tribes (35), Symbolic boundaries (49)

now.changed: Melucci (1995) and Polletta and Jasper (2001), recalled, describe collective identity negotiated inside a movement over time. Here rooms carrying a membership from before the canvas (Frame bridging, 242 rooms; Flagging the nation, 62) outnumber rooms carrying a faction formed on the canvas around a colour (Neo-tribes, 35). Members also draw a line about what may stand on the canvas (Symbolic boundaries, 49). Membership carried in does not come before the attack more often than chance (F-011).
now.mistaken_for: Social identity in the psychological sense (Tajfel and Turner, recalled), or the room's emblem. The emblem is what the room chooses to show; identity is the membership the work carries, which can exist before any emblem is chosen.

D07.why: the prose rule extended to the dimensions: 'communities that existed before it' was universal against the 78 rooms with no posts in the week before the canvas; 'what persists is chosen by the room in the last hours, not fixed by founding conditions' was a causal claim and a negative parallel that no count supports; J's ruling of 15 October (curation after hour 73) is written in; the sources are marked recalled
rests_on: J's ruling of 15 October 01:29 Berlin, ruling 1

now.changed: Stinchcombe (1965) and Marquis and Tilcsik (2013), recalled, describe how conditions at an organization's founding persist in it. Here members leave marks of the episode in their rooms near its end and after it: a celebration, a record, an emblem, ties, newcomers and, after hour 73, a curated record of the canvas (J's ruling of 15 October). Most rooms existed before the canvas; 78 of 705 have no posts in the week before it. Whether founding conditions set what persisted is not tested.

D08.why: the prose rule extended to the dimensions: 'no claim is made on any authority' was universal against members blaming moderators (5 rooms); 'the repertoire is learned in hours' was uncounted diffusion; 'often played for sport' was an uncounted comparison and now carries its count; the mistaken_for sentence now carries A16's and A17's counts

now.changed: Tilly and Tarrow (2007, recalled) describe contention as claim-making against or through authorities, with a repertoire learned over years. Here rooms contest each other's pixels within the 73 hours of placement. Members grief another room's work for fun in 13 rooms. Whether rooms learned their moves from each other is not counted.
now.mistaken_for: Conflict as the breakdown of order between rooms. Here the contest and its settlement run together inside the attacking room: the first attack call comes before the first sparing, refusal or apology in 82 of 104 rooms (A16), and before the first border talk in 95 of 172 (A17).
